prompt: Analyze has_duplicate(values) for a list of n distinct plain integers, so it never returns early. Use a CPython-style array-backed list cost model: copying k element references costs Theta(k), checking membership among k unequal integers costs Theta(k), and each integer comparison, iteration step and index operation costs constant time. Analyze only the function call, excluding construction of the example input and printing. As n grows, which option gives the tight running-time bound and a correct explanation? The displayed six-element call is only a behavior example. Theta means a tight asymptotic bound.

options.text: Theta(n squared). Each slice still returns only the requested prefix, but Python first copies all n references into a temporary list and then removes the unwanted suffix. That full copy happens on every iteration.
options.feedback: The total bound and returned prefix are right, but the alleged internal full-copy-then-trim algorithm is wrong in the stated model. Slicing copies the selected index references, not all n first. Summing those growing prefix costs still gives quadratic time.
options.partial_reason: Correct: the total bound is Theta(n squared), each returned slice is the requested prefix, and no distinct input value is found in its earlier prefix. Incorrect: claims every slice first copies all n references internally and then removes the suffix, rather than copying the selected prefix references.

options.text: Theta(n). There is only one visible loop, and both the slice and membership check can be treated as constant-time operations.
options.feedback: A single visible loop need not be linear. Under the stated model, slicing and unsuccessful membership each take time proportional to the current prefix length. Summing those costs gives quadratic time.

options.text: Theta(n squared). At index i, copying the i-element prefix and searching its i unequal elements are sequential linear operations. Their costs add, and the sum of i from 0 to n minus 1 is quadratic.
options.feedback: Correct. Every input value is distinct, so each prefix search fails and the loop completes. Per-iteration copying plus searching is Theta(i), and the sum over all prefixes is Theta(n squared).

options.text: Theta(n cubed). At index i, the linear cost of slicing must be multiplied by the linear cost of membership, giving quadratic work per iteration.
options.feedback: These operations happen one after the other, not one inside each step of the other. Add their linear costs instead of multiplying them. The per-iteration cost is linear in i, and the total is quadratic, not cubic.

options.text: Theta(n log n). Ordinary list slicing and membership each use balanced search-tree operations, so every iteration takes logarithmic time.
options.feedback: Ordinary Python lists are not balanced search trees. In the stated model, a slice copies its selected references and unsuccessful membership examines the prefix linearly. The total is quadratic.

explanation: For each index i, slicing copies i references and membership checks i distinct, unequal integers. These two costs add, giving Theta(i) work plus constant bookkeeping. Since there is no early return, i runs from 0 through n minus 1. The sum is n times (n minus 1) divided by 2, so the total is Theta(n squared). The example returning False verifies behavior only, not this asymptotic claim. The stated unit-cost model abstracts away integer bit complexity and implementation constants.

verification.rationale: The exact displayed snippet must print False for its six distinct values. The complexity answer instead needs the explicit cost model and a reviewed summation argument. A successful execution or a timing experiment is not an asymptotic proof.
verification.limitations: No machine claim of complexity proof. Assumptions cover n distinct plain integers and unit-cost comparisons, not early-return inputs, user-defined equality, unbounded integer bit costs, or all Python implementations.
